strengths: BiAlign offers a coherent, relevant extension to knowledge distillation: matching teacher preferences over demonstration subsets alongside token-level output distributions. The equations and algorithm make the central method understandable and implementable, with no additional inference cost.

Table 1 reports improvements over output alignment across all five benchmarks with both teachers. Average scores increase from 29.2 to 30.2 with the 13B teacher and from 30.0 to 31.7 with the 70B teacher. Experiments with a larger student and the Phi family provide additional evidence of transferability.

The computational controls are valuable. Section 5.2 acknowledges approximately 2.3 times the training FLOPs and compares against output alignment using additional subset data and against shorter BiAlign training. These comparisons support benefits beyond simply adding data or computation.

Extensive ablations and improved preference agreement on held-out MMLU examples support the operational effectiveness of the alignment objective. Together, the clear method and controlled empirical gains support a Findings-level contribution.
weaknesses: The paper reports no run counts, variation across seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several improvements are small: the HumanEval gains over Vanilla correspond to approximately one or two additional solved problems out of 164. Consistency across benchmarks is encouraging, but does not establish the reliability of every claimed improvement.

Reproducibility is adequate at the conceptual level but weaker for exact results. The manuscript does not link code or the constructed 12K training examples, and omits important details such as optimizer settings, sequence truncation, exact evaluation prompts and answer extraction, and QLoRA configuration. Actual evaluation splits and counts should also be distinguished from total dataset sizes.

The claim that BiAlign particularly improves complex reasoning exceeds the evidence. Table 2 compares different datasets using relative gains, which can increase simply because baseline accuracy is lower; the absolute gain on ASDiv exceeds that on GSM8K. Selected reasoning examples and teacher-preference agreement do not establish improved reasoning mechanisms or separate better use of demonstrations from general improvements after training.

The broader comparative case remains limited. Output-Align is a useful direct baseline, but the experiments do not establish advantages over stronger distillation approaches discussed in related work. Moreover, the simpler alternative ranking loss slightly outperforms the proposed formulation in Table 8. The evidence supports demonstration-preference supervision more strongly than the special merits of the particular ranking loss, limiting the case for main-conference publication.
